intro: PRP (Parallel Redundancy Protocol) sends every frame twice, over two separate local area networks (LANs): LAN A and LAN B. The receiver keeps the copy that arrives first and drops the other. When one network fails, the other copy still arrives. Nothing is lost, and nothing waits for the network to repair itself. HSR (High-availability Seamless Redundancy) does the same on a ring.
plain: Imagine sending an important letter twice, by two couriers on two different roads, and keeping whichever copy arrives first. If one road is blocked, the other copy still arrives, with no delay at all. This protocol gives a substation two separate networks and sends every message on both. Its ring version sends the two copies around one loop in opposite directions.

two.title: Two networks
two.text: The relay and the bay controller each have two network ports: one on LAN A, one on LAN B. Such a device is a DAN, a doubly attached node. The two LANs share no switch, no cable and no power supply. Every 2 s, each DAN sends a short supervision frame on both LANs to say it is there.

send.title: Send twice
send.text: The relay has a GOOSE message for the controller: a fast event message between substation devices. Its PRP layer adds a 6-byte trailer, a few bytes at the end of the frame. Then it sends one copy on each port at the same moment. This copy goes over LAN A.

drop.title: Drop the duplicate
drop.text: The copy on LAN B arrives 4 µs later. It has the same source and the same sequence number, so the controller knows it has it already and drops it. The program on the controller sees the message only once.

break.title: A cable breaks
break.text: The cable from switch A to the controller is cut. Just then, the relay trips. The copy on LAN A gets only as far as switch A. The copy on LAN B arrives as usual. Nothing is lost, nothing is late, and nothing has to switch over.

alarm.title: Alarm and repair
alarm.text: The protection noticed nothing. The controller does: its port A has no link, and the relay's frames now arrive on LAN B only. It raises an alarm. Until LAN A is repaired, one more fault would cut the relay off.

frames.sup-a: I am here, with two ports
frames.sup-b: I am here, with two ports
frames.copy-a: Heartbeat: no trip (copy on LAN A)
frames.copy-b: Heartbeat: no trip (copy on LAN B)
frames.sup-only: I am here (heard on LAN B only)

notes.sup-a: A PRP supervision frame, sent every 2 s on both LANs to 01-15-4E-00-01-00, EtherType 0x88FB. It tells the other nodes that the relay is doubly attached and that both its paths work.
notes.sup-b: The same supervision frame, sent at the same moment on LAN B.
notes.trip-a: The copy on LAN A reaches switch A. Its cable to the controller is cut, so this copy goes no further.
notes.sup-only: The relay's next supervision frame. It still leaves on both LANs, but only the copy on LAN B reaches the controller.

dst.name: Destination
dst.note: F1 PROT's GOOSE multicast address, as in the GOOSE lesson. PRP changes nothing in front of the trailer.

src.name: Source
src.note: The relay's MAC address. Both its ports use this same address, so the two copies look alike.

vlan.name: VLAN tag
vlan.note: Priority 4, VLAN 10, as in the GOOSE lesson.

ethertype.name: EtherType
ethertype.note: 0x88B8: GOOSE. PRP adds no header at the front: the trailer at the end is all it adds.

goose-header.name: GOOSE header
goose-header.note: APPID 0x0001, length 115 and two reserved fields, unchanged.

goose-pdu.name: GOOSE message
goose-pdu.note: 0x61 starts the GOOSE message; 105 bytes follow. PRP leaves all of it as it is.

gocbref.name: gocbRef
gocbref.note: F1PROTLD0/LLN0$GO$gcbTrip: the name of the control block that sends this message.

tal.name: Time allowed to live
tal.note: 2000 ms. If no copy arrives within this time, subscribers treat the data as invalid.

datset.name: datSet
datset.note: F1PROTLD0/LLN0$dsTrip: the list of values this message carries.

goid.name: goID
goid.note: F1PROT_Trip: an ID that subscribers can check.

t-old.name: t
t-old.note: 08:00:00 UTC, the time of the last change.

t-event.name: t
t-event.note: 10:41:07.232 UTC, the time of the trip.

st-12.name: stNum 12 · sqNum 3
st-12.note: Nothing has changed: the fourth copy of state 12.

st-13.name: stNum 13 · sqNum 0
st-13.note: A new state: its first copy.

flags-1.name: simulation · confRev
flags-1.note: Not a test message; configuration revision 1.

flags-2.name: ndsCom · entries
flags-2.note: Set up completely (not "needs commissioning"); 2 values follow.

seq-3900.name: Sequence number
seq-3900.note: 0x0F3C = 3900. The relay numbers every frame it sends; both copies carry the same number.

seq-3905.name: Sequence number
seq-3905.note: 0x0F41 = 3905: the relay has sent other frames since.

lan-a.name: LAN and size
lan-a.note: A: sent on LAN A. Then 0x079 = 121, the number of bytes after the EtherType, trailer included.

lan-b.name: LAN and size
lan-b.note: B: sent on LAN B. This is the only byte that differs from the copy on LAN A.

suffix.name: PRP suffix
suffix.note: 0x88FB marks the end of a PRP trailer.

a-seq.name: SeqNr
a-seq.note: 16 bits. The receiver keeps the first frame with a new number from this source and drops the second.

a-lan.name: LanId
a-lan.note: 4 bits: 1010 (A) or 1011 (B), the LAN the copy was sent on.

a-size.name: LSDUsize
a-size.note: 12 bits: 121 bytes. The receiver compares it with the real size of the frame: if they match, the last 6 bytes are a trailer. A VLAN tag is not counted, because switches may add or remove it.

a-suffix.name: PRPsuffix
a-suffix.note: 0x88FB, the same number as the EtherType of the supervision frames.

facts.standard: IEC 62439-3 (PRP in clause 4, HSR in clause 5)
facts.between: Doubly attached nodes: relays, controllers, merging units, gateways
facts.transport: Ethernet, below IP: GOOSE, SV and MMS all ride on it
facts.frames: PRP: a 6-byte trailer at the end (0x88FB). HSR: a 6-byte tag after the source address (0x892F)
facts.speed: No recovery time: no frame is lost when one LAN fails

tips: Never connect LAN A to LAN B. Keep them apart in switches, cables, colors and power. A node counts frames that arrive with the wrong LAN in their trailer: check that counter after commissioning.
A failed LAN stops nothing, so nobody notices it. Alarm on each port and on missing supervision frames, or the next failure takes everything down.
The trailer adds 6 bytes. A full-size frame (1522 bytes with a VLAN tag) becomes 1528: every switch must accept it, or the nodes must send smaller frames.
HSR has no switches in the ring: every node passes the ring's frames on. A node that is switched off opens the ring at that point, and a second one splits it.

playground.file: Try it: what the controller captured on its two ports from the relay, and how it keeps one copy of each frame.
playground.columns: What the two ports saw, frame by frame. PRP adds a trailer to each frame: its sequence number, its LAN, its size and the suffix 88 FB.
playground.first: The copy that arrives first is kept and passed up to the protection application.
playground.drop: The same source and SeqNr again, from LAN B: a duplicate, dropped. The application sees each frame once.
playground.trip: The trip, 232 ms later: SeqNr 3905. It arrives on LAN B first and is kept.
playground.lost: Its copy on LAN A never comes: the cable is cut. Nothing is lost and nothing switches over; the trip was already through.
playground.supervision: Each LAN carries a supervision frame every 2 s. Only LAN B's arrives, so the controller raises the alarm that LAN A is down.
playground.trailer: The 6 bytes of the trailer: SeqNr 0F 3C = 3900, LAN A (the nibble A) and the size 0x079 = 121 bytes, then the suffix 88 FB.
